knowledgeUnits.heading: Binary and decimal prefixes use different scales

leadVisual.title: The storage ladder

coreExplanation: Binary prefixes use powers of 1024: kibi (Ki) means 2^10, mebi (Mi) means 2^20, gibi (Gi) means 2^30 and tebi (Ti) means 2^40. Therefore 1 KiB = 1024 bytes, 1 MiB = 2^20 bytes, 1 GiB = 2^30 bytes and 1 TiB = 2^40 bytes.

Decimal prefixes use powers of 1000: kilo (k) means 10^3, mega (M) means 10^6, giga (G) means 10^9 and tera (T) means 10^12. Therefore 1 kB = 1000 bytes, 1 MB = 10^6 bytes, 1 GB = 10^9 bytes and 1 TB = 10^12 bytes. Case and the i in KiB/MiB/GiB/TiB carry meaning.
Binary prefixes climb by 1024; decimal prefixes climb by 1000.
A binary staircase has 1024 steps per level; a decimal staircase has 1000. The labels tell you which staircase to climb.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Binary

leadVisual.title: 8-bit binary place values

coreExplanation: Binary is a base-2 number system. It uses only the digits 0 and 1.
Each position has a place value that is a power of 2. Starting at the right, the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 and so on; a 1 includes its place value and a 0 does not.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Denary

leadVisual.title: Denary place values

coreExplanation: Denary is a base-10 number system. It uses the digits 0 to 9.
Each position has a place value that is a power of 10. Starting at the right, the place values are 1, 10, 100, 1000 and so on.

workedExample.title: Read a denary numeral by place value

knowledgeUnits.heading: Hexadecimal

leadVisual.title: Why hexadecimal is used

coreExplanation: Hexadecimal is a base-16 number system. It uses the digits 0 to 9 followed by A, B, C, D, E and F, which represent the digit values 10 to 15.
Each position has a place value that is a power of 16. Starting at the right, the place values are 1, 16, 256, 4096 and so on.

Hexadecimal is used as a compact way for people to read long binary patterns. One hexadecimal digit represents four binary bits, so it is practical for memory addresses, machine-code or debugging values, and colour codes.

workedExample.title: Read a hexadecimal numeral by place value

knowledgeUnits.heading: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD)

leadVisual.title: BCD keeps denary digits separate

coreExplanation: Binary Coded Decimal (BCD) is a representation in which each denary digit is encoded separately as a four-bit group. Only 0000 to 1001 are valid BCD digit groups because a single denary digit can only be 0 to 9.

BCD is used when individual decimal digits must be preserved for exact input, processing or display, such as in a digital clock or calculator. This makes digit handling direct, although BCD normally uses more bits than a pure binary representation of the same integer.

workedExample.title: Encode the denary digits 407 in BCD

knowledgeUnits.heading: One's complement

leadVisual.title: Why one's complement appeared

coreExplanation: One's complement represents a negative fixed-width binary integer by inverting every bit of the positive value: each 0 becomes 1 and each 1 becomes 0.

It is used to represent negative values and makes sign reversal a direct bit inversion. Its drawback is that it has two zero patterns, one positive and one negative, which makes zero testing and arithmetic less convenient.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Two's complement

leadVisual.title: Why two's complement replaced one's complement

coreExplanation: Two's complement represents a negative fixed-width binary integer by inverting every bit of the positive value and then adding 1 to the inverted pattern.

It is used because it provides one representation of zero and lets the same fixed-width binary addition circuitry handle positive and negative integers. In 8 bits, its representable range is −128 to +127.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Conversion between number systems and representations

leadVisual.title: Binary, denary and hexadecimal conversions

coreExplanation: A conversion preserves the integer value while changing the number base or representation. Identify the source, destination and any required bit width before choosing a method.

Use powers of 2 for binary and denary, four-bit nibbles for binary and hexadecimal, powers of 16 for hexadecimal and denary, separate four-bit digit groups for BCD, and fixed-width inversion rules for one's complement and two's complement.
When there is no convenient direct route, convert through denary or binary as an intermediate representation, then reverse the route to check that the value has not changed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unsigned binary addition and subtraction

leadVisual.title: Unsigned binary addition

coreExplanation: An unsigned binary integer uses every bit as a non-negative place value. An unsigned 8-bit value represents an integer from 0 to 255.
For addition, align equal-width operands and work from the rightmost bit to the left. Use 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, 1 + 1 = 10 and 1 + 1 + 1 = 11, carrying 1 into the next column when required.

For unsigned subtraction, align equal-width operands and borrow from the next column when the upper bit is smaller than the lower bit. A negative mathematical result cannot be represented as an unsigned value.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Overflow in fixed-width arithmetic

leadVisual.title: Unsigned 8-bit overflow

coreExplanation: Overflow occurs when the true mathematical result is outside the range that the stated bit width and representation can store. The stored bit pattern then cannot represent the true result.
For unsigned 8-bit addition, the permitted range is 0 to 255. A carry beyond the eighth bit shows that the true result needs nine bits; only the rightmost eight bits fit in the register.
A leftmost stored bit of 1 is not by itself overflow. For example, 01111111 + 00000001 = 10000000 represents 128 and still fits in the unsigned 8-bit range.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Signed binary addition and subtraction

leadVisual.title: Signed two's-complement addition

coreExplanation: Signed arithmetic extends the same fixed-width column addition method to positive and negative integers. Encode every negative operand in the stated signed representation before calculating.
With two's-complement operands, add every column including the most-significant bit and discard any carry beyond the fixed width. Interpret the retained result as a two's-complement value.
To calculate A − B, form the two's complement of B and add it to A at the same width. For signed 8-bit arithmetic, the final mathematical result must remain in the range −128 to +127.
For two's-complement addition, operands with the same sign that produce a retained result with the opposite sign indicate overflow. Confirm this by comparing the exact result with the signed range.

leadVisual.title: From character to stored bits

coreExplanation: A character set defines a collection of characters and assigns a numeric character code to each character. The code identifies the character independently of how a font draws it on screen.
The numeric code is stored internally as a binary bit pattern. Software must use the agreed character set or encoding to interpret the stored bits as the intended character.

knowledgeUnits.heading: ASCII

leadVisual.title: Standard ASCII capacity

coreExplanation: Standard ASCII is a 7-bit character set, so it provides 2⁷ = 128 possible character codes numbered 0 to 127.
Its repertoire includes common English letters, digits, punctuation and control characters. The limited number of codes means it cannot represent the full range of writing systems used worldwide.

workedExample.title: Check whether a supplied code fits standard ASCII

knowledgeUnits.heading: Extended ASCII

leadVisual.title: Extended ASCII capacity

coreExplanation: Extended ASCII uses 8-bit character codes, so it provides 2⁸ = 256 possible code values numbered 0 to 255.

The additional codes can represent extra accented letters and symbols, but 256 values are still insufficient for all world writing systems. Different extended-ASCII code pages may assign different characters to some of the added code values.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unicode

leadVisual.title: Unicode supports global character repertoires

coreExplanation: Unicode assigns code points to characters from a very wide range of languages, symbol systems and modern character collections. This makes it suitable for multilingual data and communication.
Unicode code points can be stored using encodings such as UTF-8 or UTF-16. It is inaccurate to claim that every Unicode character is always stored using exactly the same number of bits.

knowledgeUnits.heading: How a bitmap image is stored

leadVisual.title: Decode every pixel at its original position

coreExplanation: A bitmap image is represented as a rectangular grid of picture elements. The file stores an ordered colour value for every pixel, row by row or in another defined order.

The file header stores metadata needed to interpret the pixel data, such as width, height, colour depth and file type. Software reads the header and then uses the ordered pixel values to reconstruct the image correctly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pixel

leadVisual.title: What is a pixel?

coreExplanation: A pixel is one picture element in a bitmap. Each pixel occupies one position in the stored image grid and is assigned one colour value.
A pixel is a data element rather than a fixed physical size. How large it appears depends on the display size and the relationship between the image and screen resolutions.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Colour depth

leadVisual.title: Compare colour depth at a fixed image resolution

coreExplanation: Colour depth is the number of bits used to store the colour of each pixel. A colour depth of n bits provides 2ⁿ possible bit patterns and therefore up to 2ⁿ possible colours.

Increasing colour depth can represent colours more accurately and reduce visible banding, but it stores more bits for every pixel. At the same image resolution, a higher colour depth therefore increases the uncompressed file size.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Image resolution

leadVisual.title: Image resolution: width × height

coreExplanation: Image resolution is the number of pixels used to represent the stored image, normally stated as width × height. For the same subject and colour depth, a higher image resolution records more spatial detail because more pixel positions are available.
More pixels also increase the uncompressed file size. Screen resolution instead describes the pixel dimensions of a display; it does not state how many pixels are stored in a particular image file.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Uncompressed bitmap file size

leadVisual.title: Uncompressed bitmap file size

coreExplanation: The uncompressed bitmap pixel-data size in bits is width × height × colour depth. Width × height gives the number of pixels, and colour depth gives the bits stored for each pixel.
Divide the bit total by 8 to convert bits to bytes. This basic calculation excludes file-header overhead unless the question supplies an additional header size.

knowledgeUnits.heading: How a vector graphic is stored

leadVisual.title: How a vector graphic is stored

coreExplanation: A vector graphic is encoded as a drawing list. Each entry defines a drawing object and properties such as its type, coordinates, dimensions, line colour, fill colour and line thickness.
When the graphic is displayed, software reads the list in order and redraws the objects from their stored properties. The file does not store a fixed colour value for every position in a pixel grid.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Bitmap and vector enlargement

leadVisual.title: Enlarging bitmap and vector graphics

coreExplanation: Enlarging a bitmap spreads a fixed grid of stored pixels over a larger area. Individual square pixels can become visible and curved or diagonal edges may look jagged or pixelated.

A vector graphic is redrawn from its objects and properties at the new size, so its curves and edges remain smooth. Choose vector for logos and diagrams that must scale cleanly; choose bitmap for detailed continuous-tone photographs where each pixel records colour variation.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Analogue sound and the sampling process

leadVisual.title: From continuous sound to digital samples

coreExplanation: Sound in air is an analogue wave whose amplitude changes continuously. A computer creates a digital representation by measuring the wave amplitude at regular time intervals.
Each measurement is quantised to the nearest available amplitude level. The selected level is then encoded as a binary sample value, and the ordered sample values form the stored digital sound.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sampling rate

leadVisual.title: Sampling rate: samples per second

coreExplanation: Sampling rate is the number of samples taken each second, measured in hertz (Hz). A higher sampling rate records the wave at more points in the same time interval.

More frequent measurements can represent changes over time more accurately. At the same sampling resolution, number of channels and duration, a higher sampling rate stores more sample values and therefore increases file size.

The accuracy benefit describes taking new measurements of the analogue source. Resampling an existing digital recording at a higher rate interpolates additional values but cannot recover information absent from the original capture.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Sampling resolution

leadVisual.title: Sampling resolution: bits per sample

coreExplanation: Sampling resolution is the number of bits used to store each sample. A resolution of n bits provides 2ⁿ available amplitude levels.

More levels reduce the difference between a measured amplitude and the selected quantised level, improving amplitude accuracy. At the same sampling rate, channel count and duration, more bits per sample increase file size.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why files are compressed

leadVisual.title: Why files are compressed

coreExplanation: Compression reduces the number of bits needed to represent a file. Smaller files require less storage space and fewer bits must be sent across a network.
At the same data-transfer rate, sending fewer bits can reduce transfer or download time. For the same transfer time, the smaller amount of data requires less bandwidth capacity.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossy compression and different file types

leadVisual.title: Lossy compression: effect on file types

coreExplanation: Lossy compression permanently removes selected information, so the original file cannot be reconstructed exactly. It is suitable only when the intended use can tolerate a controlled reduction in fidelity.

Lossy text is unsuitable when every character must remain exact. A bitmap can lose fine detail or colour precision; a vector drawing can lose or simplify objects and properties; sound can lose less perceptible detail. Stronger loss may reduce size further but can produce visible or audible artefacts.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossless compression and different file types

leadVisual.title: Lossless compression: effect on file types

coreExplanation: Lossless compression stores a reversible representation from which every original bit can be reconstructed. No source information is discarded.

It is required for ordinary text when every character matters and for any bitmap, vector graphic or sound master that must be reproduced exactly. Repeated patterns, pixels, object properties or sample values can be encoded more compactly, although the reduction depends on the data.

For a bitmap, RLE can store a repeated colour as a count and colour code. Repeated sound sample values can also use reversible run coding; other lossless encoders exploit sample patterns while preserving every value. The format must specify how its codes are decoded.

workedExample.title: Replace repeated text with dictionary references

knowledgeUnits.heading: Lossless and lossy compression compared

leadVisual.title: Lossless and lossy compression

coreExplanation: Choose lossless compression when exact reconstruction is required. Choose lossy compression only when some permanent information loss is acceptable for the intended use.

Lossy compression often produces a greater size reduction because it can discard selected detail. The decision must balance required fidelity, expected size reduction, file content and whether the output is a master copy or a delivery copy.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Run-length encoding (RLE)

leadVisual.title: Run-length encoding (RLE)

coreExplanation: Run-length encoding is a lossless method for adjacent identical data items. It replaces each run with a count followed by the repeated value or code; decoding repeats the value by its stored count to reconstruct the original exactly.
RLE is effective when long runs save more bits than the count-and-value pairs require. Frequent changes create many short runs, and the added count for each run can make the encoded data larger.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Networking creates shared access; LAN and WAN describe scope

leadVisual.title: LAN and WAN describe network scope

coreExplanation: Networking devices connect systems so authorised users can share files, printers, storage, applications and an internet connection. Networks also support communication, collaboration, central account management and central backup.

A benefit needs a cause and a consequence. For example, storing one managed copy of an examination file on a server allows authorised users to access the current version and lets administrators back it up centrally.

A LAN covers a limited geographical area such as one building or site and is normally owned or managed by one organisation. A WAN covers a large geographical area, links separate sites or LANs and commonly uses telecommunications-provider infrastructure. These terms do not guarantee a particular speed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Network models describe who requests and who provides

leadVisual.title: Client-server and peer-to-peer assign different roles

coreExplanation: In a client-server model, clients request services or resources and one or more servers provide and manage them. Server roles may include authentication, file storage, web hosting, printing and backup.
In a peer-to-peer model, each peer may request and provide resources directly. No dedicated server is required, but accounts, security, backup and availability are distributed across peers.
A justified choice links the scenario to number of users, trust, central control, required availability, administration and cost. A topology name cannot replace a model choice.

workedExample.title: Choose a model for shared accounts

knowledgeUnits.heading: Thin and thick describe where the client work happens

leadVisual.title: Thin and thick clients place processing in different locations

coreExplanation: A thin client relies mainly on a server for processing and/or storage. It can use lower-specification hardware and supports central software management, but it depends heavily on the server and network.

A thick client performs more processing locally and normally stores more applications or data locally. It can continue more work when disconnected, but updates, security and maintenance are distributed across devices.
Thin/thick is not a synonym for client-server/peer-to-peer. It describes processing placement within a system design.

knowledgeUnits.heading: The topology is the link pattern

leadVisual.title: Count links first; trace the path second

coreExplanation: A bus connects devices to one shared backbone. A signal travels along the common medium and attached devices inspect it.
A star gives each end device a separate link to one central switch. A frame travels from the source to the switch and then from the switch to the destination link.

A mesh provides multiple interconnections. A full mesh connects every node pair directly; partial meshes retain several, but not all, possible links. Alternative connected routes may remain after one link fails.

A hybrid combines two or more topology patterns. In the example, end devices form stars around S1 and S2, while S1, S2 and S3 form a mesh. A frame is a unit of LAN data; switches forward it on selected links. Assume a loop-free forwarding path, with a spare path available after a failure.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A good choice connects structure to consequence

leadVisual.title: Topology choices create cost and failure consequences

coreExplanation: A star usually isolates one end-device cable failure, but the central switch is a single point of failure for that star.
A bus uses less cable but shares the backbone and traffic; a backbone break can divide or stop the network.
A mesh can offer alternative routes, but extra links and ports increase cost, installation and management.
A hybrid can match different areas, but its failure behaviour depends on the constituent topologies and the links joining them.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Cloud computing provides remote resources through a network

leadVisual.title: A cloud request crosses local and provider infrastructure

coreExplanation: Cloud computing provides storage, processing, applications or platforms from remote infrastructure accessed through a network. The organisation uses the service without operating every physical server locally.

A client sends a request across its local network and the internet to provider infrastructure. A virtual server or managed service performs the requested processing or storage operation and returns the result.
Cloud describes where computing resources are provided and accessed; it does not mean that data has no physical location. The resources run on physical provider or organisation-controlled hardware.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A public cloud uses shared third-party provider infrastructure

leadVisual.title: A public cloud uses shared provider infrastructure

coreExplanation: A public cloud is operated by a third-party provider. Its underlying physical resources serve multiple customers, while virtualisation, accounts and permissions provide logical separation between customers.
Public cloud describes provider control and multi-customer tenancy. It does not mean that files are open to the public; authentication, permissions and encryption are still required.

Because the provider owns and operates the shared platform, a customer can obtain resources without purchasing all of the underlying hardware but accepts greater dependence on the provider's service and controls.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

leadVisual.title: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation

coreExplanation: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation. It may be operated by that organisation on its own premises or hosted and managed on its behalf by another provider.
Private describes single-organisation tenancy and the potential for greater control or configuration. It does not require every server to be in the organisation's building.

Dedicated infrastructure can support control or compliance requirements, but it usually brings greater cost or management responsibility and still requires authentication, permissions, encryption and backup.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Cloud benefits and risks must be connected to dependence

leadVisual.title: Cloud benefits and risks arise from remote shared infrastructure

coreExplanation: Benefits can include access from different locations, collaboration, elastic capacity, reduced local hardware, provider maintenance and geographically redundant infrastructure.

Drawbacks can include dependence on broadband and the provider, recurring cost, less direct control, migration difficulty, service outage, data-location/compliance concerns and exposure if accounts or provider controls fail.

A choice depends on sensitivity, required control, expected demand, staff expertise, budget, connection resilience and legal requirements. Cloud storage is not automatically a complete backup strategy.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Wired and wireless create different constraints

leadVisual.title: Wired and wireless links create different constraints

coreExplanation: Wired devices send signals through a physical cable. A cable provides a guided path and can offer stable high capacity and reduced exposure to radio interference, but installation restricts movement and may require building work.

Wireless devices send electromagnetic waves through space. This supports mobility and flexible installation, but range, obstacles, competing signals and unauthorised reception attempts must be managed.
Security is not guaranteed by either category. Wired links still need access control and wireless links need strong authentication and encryption.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Copper cable, fibre-optic cable and radio waves including WiFi

leadVisual.title: Transmission media carry signals in different physical forms

coreExplanation: Copper cable carries changing electrical signals. It is widely available and relatively inexpensive, but suffers attenuation and can be affected by electromagnetic interference; shielding and twisted pairs reduce interference.

Fibre-optic cable carries pulses of light through glass or plastic. It supports high data capacity, low attenuation over long distances and immunity to electromagnetic interference, but equipment and installation can cost more and the fibre needs careful handling.

Radio waves, including WiFi, carry data through space and provide mobility within a coverage area. They can pass through some obstacles, but distance, walls, competing transmitters and shared spectrum can weaken the signal or reduce capacity. Wireless access must use authentication and encryption because signals can extend beyond the intended room or building.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Microwaves

leadVisual.title: Microwaves: direction and line of sight

coreExplanation: Microwaves are high-frequency electromagnetic waves. A narrow, directional beam can carry data between fixed antennas at two sites, providing a high-bandwidth point-to-point link without installing cable between the sites.

The transmitting and receiving antennas must be accurately aligned and normally need a clear line of sight. Buildings, hills and the curvature of the Earth can block the signal, so tall masts or relay stations may be needed over a long distance.

Microwaves are useful between buildings or across ground where laying cable is difficult or expensive. Interference, movement of an antenna and bad weather can weaken the signal and make the link less reliable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Satellites

leadVisual.title: Satellites: uplink, downlink and coverage

coreExplanation: A ground station sends microwaves to a satellite using an uplink. The satellite receives the signal and sends it back to one or more receiving dishes using a downlink.

Satellites can cover a very large geographical area and reach ships, aircraft and remote locations where installing cable is difficult or impossible. The same transmission can also be sent across a wide area.

Signals travel a very long distance to and from a satellite, so there is a time delay. This can affect telephone calls, video conferencing and real-time control. Bad weather can weaken the signal, and satellite equipment and services can be expensive.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Selecting a transmission medium from the scenario

leadVisual.title: Medium selection matrix

coreExplanation: Choose a transmission medium by matching its physical carrier and operating characteristics to the scenario. Relevant factors include distance, required bandwidth, attenuation, interference, mobility, line of sight, time delay, installation constraints, security controls and cost.

A justified choice states the medium, names a specific characteristic and explains the consequence in the given setting. For example, fibre suits a long link near electrical machinery because light transmission is not affected by electromagnetic interference; satellites suit a remote vessel because their wide coverage does not require cable to be installed along the whole route.

leadVisual.title: Each LAN device has a distinct networking role

coreExplanation: A NIC connects a device to a wired network; a WNIC connects it wirelessly. A wireless access point (WAP) bridges wireless devices into the wired LAN. Cables carry signals between wired interfaces.
A switch learns and uses link-layer addresses to forward frames to the required LAN port. A server provides network services or resources such as authentication, files, printing or web content.
These devices perform different jobs even when several functions share one physical case. Name the device and the exact forwarding, connection or service role it performs.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A bridge connects and filters between LAN segments

leadVisual.title: A bridge connects and filters between LAN segments

coreExplanation: A bridge connects LAN segments and learns which link-layer or MAC addresses are reachable through each side. It uses that information to decide whether a frame needs to cross the bridge.
A frame whose destination remains on its source segment is filtered rather than copied to the other segment. A frame required on the other segment is forwarded across the bridge.
A bridge makes a link-layer forwarding decision inside a LAN; it does not replace the router that forwards IP packets between different networks.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A repeater regenerates a weakened signal

leadVisual.title: A repeater regenerates a weakened signal

coreExplanation: As a signal travels through a medium, attenuation and distortion can make it too weak or unclear to continue reliably. A repeater receives that weakened signal and regenerates the intended signal pattern.
The restored signal is retransmitted so it can travel farther along the network medium. The repeater extends the usable transmission distance; it does not create a new destination.
A repeater does not inspect a MAC or IP destination and does not choose a route. Its job is signal regeneration rather than selective forwarding.

knowledgeUnits.heading: The router crosses a network boundary

leadVisual.title: A router forwards packets between different networks

coreExplanation: A router connects different networks. It inspects the destination IP address, consults routing information and forwards the packet toward the next network or next hop.

A switch normally decides which LAN port should receive a frame; a router decides which network path should receive a packet. A home device may combine switch, WAP, router and modem functions in one case, but the roles remain distinct.

knowledgeUnits.heading: CSMA/CD detects a collision, stops, waits and retries

leadVisual.title: CSMA/CD detects a collision and retries after a random delay

coreExplanation: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3) carries data in frames on many wired LANs. On a traditional shared or half-duplex Ethernet medium, two stations can begin transmitting close together and their signals can collide.

CSMA/CD means Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection. A station listens first, transmits if the medium is idle, monitors for collision, stops and sends/recognises a jam signal if a collision occurs, waits for a random backoff period and then tries again.

Independent random waits reduce the chance that both stations retry at the same instant, but the selected waits may be equal and another collision may occur. CSMA/CD does not guarantee that a collision never happens; modern switched full-duplex Ethernet normally gives separate collision-free links, but the syllabus mechanism models the shared-medium case.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Streaming begins before the complete media file arrives

leadVisual.title: Streaming starts playback before the complete file arrives

coreExplanation: Bit streaming delivers an ordered flow of media data progressively so playback can begin before the complete file has arrived.
On-demand streaming sends stored content chosen by the user; the user controls when to begin. Real-time streaming sends content as it is produced, such as a live event, with minimal practical delay.
Both methods may use a buffer. ‘Real-time’ does not mean zero delay, and ‘on-demand’ does not require downloading the complete file first.

knowledgeUnits.heading: The buffer level is the difference between two rates over time

leadVisual.title: Reservoir analogy: fill rate, stored level and drain rate

coreExplanation: Bit rate is the number of bits transmitted or consumed each second. The incoming rate is limited by available broadband capacity and current conditions; the playback bit rate is how quickly the media player consumes encoded data.

A buffer stores data that has arrived but has not yet been played. If incoming rate exceeds playback bit rate, the level rises. If the rates are equal, the level is stable. If incoming rate is lower, the buffer drains.

A buffer absorbs short variation. If the deficit continues, stored data reaches zero and playback must pause or switch to a lower-bit-rate version. More buffer increases the time before interruption but does not repair sustained insufficient speed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: The internet carries many services; the WWW is one

leadVisual.title: The World Wide Web is one service carried by the internet

coreExplanation: The internet is the global network of interconnected networks, routers and transmission links that carries data using common protocols.
The World Wide Web is one service using that infrastructure. It provides linked resources identified by URLs and normally accessed with browsers and web protocols.
Email, file transfer, online games and voice/video communication can use the internet without being WWW resources. A failed web service does not imply that every internet service has failed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A modem modulates and demodulates signals

leadVisual.title: A modem adapts signals for the access link

coreExplanation: A modem is a modulator-demodulator. For a telephone-line connection, it converts digital data into an analogue signal suitable for transmission and converts received analogue signals back into digital data.

Modulation represents outgoing digital data in an analogue carrier signal. Demodulation recovers digital data from the incoming analogue signal. Keep both directions in an explanation of a modem used with the PSTN.
The modem does not inspect the destination IP address or choose the next network path. That routing decision belongs to the router even when a consumer device combines both functions in one case.

knowledgeUnits.heading: PSTN carries signals through switched fixed telephone lines

leadVisual.title: PSTN carries signals through switched telephone lines

coreExplanation: PSTN means Public Switched Telephone Network. It is the fixed telephone system formed from telephone lines, cables and telephone exchanges that establish a switched path between connected endpoints.
A home telephone connects through a fixed telephone line to a telephone exchange. Further exchanges can switch the call or signal through the PSTN to another connected telephone line.

A computer can use a modem or access equipment to send data through a suitable telephone-line service. The modem is the endpoint conversion device; the PSTN is the wider switched telephone-line network.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A dedicated line reserves a connection for one customer or site

leadVisual.title: A dedicated line reserves a provider connection

coreExplanation: A dedicated line provides a permanent or reserved provider connection for one customer or site rather than establishing a temporary connection only when required.
Reserved capacity can give predictable availability, performance or site-to-site connectivity, which can suit an organisation with continuous or critical communication requirements.
The organisation normally pays higher installation and recurring costs. A sound choice connects that extra cost to the scenario's need for predictable permanent connectivity.

knowledgeUnits.heading: A cell phone network provides mobile radio access

leadVisual.title: A cell phone network provides mobile radio access

coreExplanation: A cell phone or cellular network connects a mobile device by radio to a base station. The base station passes the traffic into the cellular provider network and onward to wider networks.
As the user moves, the device can connect through available coverage areas and may transfer between base stations. This provides mobility without a fixed telephone line to the device.

Availability and performance depend on coverage, distance, obstacles, interference, radio conditions and capacity shared with other users. A recommendation must test those constraints against the scenario.

knowledgeUnits.heading: An IP address identifies a network interface for routing

leadVisual.title: Read version and interface separately

coreExplanation: IPv4 addresses contain 32 bits and are normally written as four decimal octets, each from 0 to 255, such as 192.0.2.37.
IPv6 addresses contain 128 bits and are normally written as eight groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons, such as 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0042.

An IP address is associated with a network interface on a network. A device with wired and wireless interfaces can have different IP addresses, and a dynamically assigned address may change over time.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Subnetting decides whether delivery is local or routed

leadVisual.title: Subnetting decides local delivery or router forwarding

coreExplanation: Subnetting divides an address space into smaller logical networks so an organisation can allocate and manage address groups. A host compares its own network prefix with the destination network prefix: a matching prefix means local delivery; a different prefix requires a router.

With a /24 prefix, the first 24 bits identify the network. For 192.168.10.37/24, destination 192.168.10.80 shares the network prefix and is local; destination 192.168.11.80 has a different prefix and must be sent to a router.

A /n prefix reserves the first n of the 32 IPv4 bits for the network and leaves 32 − n host bits. The subnet mask has n leading 1s followed by 0s. Bitwise AND of an address and its mask gives the subnet address. For /26, the mask is 255.255.255.192: the final octet is 11000000, leaving six host bits and blocks of 64 addresses. Subnet membership is separate from public/private scope and static/dynamic assignment.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Public and private IP addresses describe routing scope

leadVisual.title: Public and private IP addresses describe routing scope

coreExplanation: A public IP address is routable on the public internet. Public describes routing scope; it does not mean that every service at the address must be open to every user.

A private IP address is used inside a local network and is not routed directly across the public internet. Private interfaces commonly reach public networks through network address translation (NAT) at a router.
Private addressing reduces direct public reachability but does not guarantee security. Firewalls, authentication, updates, encryption and permissions remain necessary.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Static and dynamic IP addresses describe assignment lifetime

leadVisual.title: Static and dynamic IP addresses describe assignment lifetime

coreExplanation: A static IP address remains assigned until it is deliberately changed. This suits a server or printer that clients must find predictably at the same address.
A dynamic IP address is assigned for a lease, commonly by DHCP. The service simplifies address management for ordinary client devices, and the address may change between leases.
Static/dynamic describes assignment lifetime, not routing scope. A static address can be private, and a dynamic address can be public.

knowledgeUnits.heading: DNS resolves the domain name; the browser requests the web page or file

leadVisual.title: A URL and DNS locate one WWW resource

coreExplanation: A Uniform Resource Locator (URL) is a text-based address used to identify and locate a resource on the World Wide Web. In https://learn.example.org/course/page.html, https is the protocol, learn.example.org is the domain name and course/page.html is the web page or file name.
The Domain Name Service (DNS) resolves the domain name to an IP address. DNS does not resolve the complete URL, store the web page or return the requested resource.
After DNS returns the IP address, the browser contacts the web server at that address, requests the web page or file named by the URL and receives the WWW resource from the server.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Laser printer

leadVisual.title: Laser printer: principal operation

coreExplanation: A photosensitive drum receives a uniform electrostatic charge. A laser scans the drum and creates a charge pattern representing the page; toner is attracted to the required parts of that pattern.
The toner image transfers from the drum to paper. Heated pressure rollers fuse the toner permanently to the paper.

knowledgeUnits.heading: 3D printer

leadVisual.title: 3D printer: principal operation

coreExplanation: Software divides a digital three-dimensional model into thin layers. The printer follows the data for one layer at a time and deposits or solidifies material at the required positions.
The print head or build platform moves between layers. Successive layers bond or solidify until they form the physical object.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Microphone

leadVisual.title: Microphone: principal operation

coreExplanation: Sound waves make a diaphragm vibrate. A transducer converts these movements into a varying analogue electrical signal that represents the sound wave.
For a computer to store or process the sound, an analogue-to-digital converter samples and quantises the signal and encodes the sample values as binary data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Speakers

leadVisual.title: Speakers: principal operation

coreExplanation: A digital-to-analogue converter changes stored binary sample values into a varying analogue signal. An amplifier supplies sufficient current to drive the speaker.
The signal in the voice coil produces a changing magnetic field that interacts with a permanent magnet. The coil and attached cone move, vibrating the air to create sound waves.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Magnetic hard disk

leadVisual.title: Magnetic hard disk: principal operation

coreExplanation: Magnetic platters rotate while an actuator positions a read/write head above the required track. The required sector passes beneath the head as the platter turns.
To write, the head changes the magnetic orientation of small areas that represent bits. To read, the head senses the stored magnetic pattern and the controller decodes it as binary data.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Solid-state flash memory

leadVisual.title: Solid-state flash memory: principal operation

coreExplanation: Flash memory stores charge in floating-gate transistor cells. The presence or amount of trapped charge changes a cell's threshold behaviour and represents stored bit values.
A controller applies voltages to program or erase cells and detects their charge state when reading. Because storage is electronic, flash memory has no moving mechanical parts.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Optical disc reader/writer

leadVisual.title: Optical disc reader/writer: principal operation

coreExplanation: The drive spins the disc and focuses a low-power laser on a track. A detector senses differences in reflected light, and the controller converts those changes into binary data.
For a recordable disc, a higher-power laser changes areas of the recording layer. The changed and unchanged areas produce distinguishable optical states when the disc is read.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Touchscreen

leadVisual.title: Touchscreen: principal operation

coreExplanation: A capacitive touchscreen maintains an electric field across a transparent electrode grid. A finger touching the screen changes the local capacitance or electric field.
The controller detects the change at the electrodes and calculates the touch coordinates. The display provides visual output while the touch-sensitive layer provides input.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Virtual-reality headset

leadVisual.title: Virtual-reality headset: principal operation

coreExplanation: The headset displays a separate viewpoint for each eye so the user perceives depth. Lenses place the displays in the user's field of view, and speakers or headphones can provide corresponding sound output.
Motion and orientation sensors detect head movement. The computer uses the sensor data to update the rendered viewpoint, so the displayed scene appears to follow the user's movement.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Buffers absorb temporary differences in transfer rate

leadVisual.title: Follow the waiting blocks

coreExplanation: A buffer is an area of memory holding data temporarily during transfer between components or devices. It allows a burst from a sender to wait while a receiver consumes the data at its own rate.

Buffer capacity is finite. If incoming data continues to arrive faster than it is removed, the buffer eventually fills; the sender must wait or data may be lost. Buffering does not increase the receiver's sustained operating rate.

A printer can receive blocks into a buffer while the processor performs other work. A device driver translates device-specific commands, and a print queue orders waiting jobs; these have different roles from the temporary data storage itself.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why RAM changes while ROM remains stable

leadVisual.title: RAM and ROM

coreExplanation: RAM is read/write primary memory used for programs and data currently being processed. Its contents change as programs start, data is edited and intermediate results are produced; ordinary RAM is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is removed.

ROM is non-volatile primary memory used for instructions that must remain available when power is removed, such as firmware or start-up instructions. During normal operation its contents are read rather than repeatedly changed, so they remain stable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: SRAM and DRAM: storage method, performance and use

leadVisual.title: Powered latch or refreshed charge

coreExplanation: SRAM stores each bit in a flip-flop circuit and does not need refresh while power is supplied. It is fast but uses more components per bit, giving lower density and higher cost per bit, so it is used for processor cache.
DRAM stores each bit as charge in a capacitor. Charge leaks, so the cells require periodic refresh; DRAM is slower but denser and cheaper per bit, so it is used for large-capacity main memory.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Monitoring and control systems compared

leadVisual.title: Monitoring and control

coreExplanation: A monitoring system uses sensors to collect data for recording, display or an alert. It reports the measured condition and does not necessarily change it.
A control system uses sensor data and a stored rule or target to decide an output. It sends an output signal to an actuator, which changes the physical condition.

coreExplanation: Select a sensor by matching the physical quantity it detects to the data required by the system. The official syllabus names temperature, pressure, infra-red and sound sensors.

knowledgeUnits.heading: How sensors, a microprocessor and actuators form a control system

leadVisual.title: Sensor, microprocessor and actuator flow

coreExplanation: A sensor measures a physical condition and sends a signal representing the reading. If the signal is analogue, an ADC converts it into digital data before a microprocessor can process it.

The microprocessor compares the reading with a stored target or rule and sends an output signal to an actuator. The actuator converts that signal into a physical action, such as operating a motor, heater, valve or alarm.

knowledgeUnits.heading: The importance of feedback

leadVisual.title: Why feedback matters

coreExplanation: Feedback is a new sensor reading obtained after an actuator has changed the physical condition. It tells the controller the actual effect of the previous output rather than assuming that the required change occurred.

By repeatedly comparing new readings with the target, the controller can continue, adjust or stop the actuator. Without feedback, a disturbance or an ineffective actuator could leave the condition away from the target with no automatic correction.

AND requires both inputs to be 1. OR includes any case with at least one 1. XOR, also called EOR, accepts exactly one 1: its output is 0 when the two inputs are equal.
An output circle denotes inversion. NAND complements the complete AND result; NOR complements the complete OR result. The extra curved line on the input side distinguishes XOR from OR.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Von Neumann architecture and the stored program concept

leadVisual.title: Processor and shared memory

coreExplanation: A stored program computer holds its instructions in memory. The processor fetches these instructions, decodes them and carries out the specified operations. Loading another instruction sequence changes the task the computer performs.

The basic Von Neumann model uses one memory for instructions and data. The processor contains a control unit, an arithmetic and logic unit and registers. Buses connect the processor to memory and input/output interfaces; instructions and data share transfer paths.

workedExample.title: A program and its data in one store

knowledgeUnits.heading: General-purpose and special-purpose registers

leadVisual.title: Register roles

coreExplanation: Registers are small, fast storage locations inside the processor. A general-purpose register can hold operands and intermediate results; a special-purpose register has a defined role. In CPU architecture, ACC has the designated accumulator role and appears with the special-purpose registers. In the syllabus's example assembly model, ACC is also the only register available for general data operations; IX supplies an index offset.

During instruction processing, several registers are needed at once: one identifies the next instruction, one retains the current instruction, and others support memory transfers. Status flags record conditions such as zero, carry, sign or overflow, depending on the processor; they are not the complete arithmetic answer.

knowledgeUnits.heading: ALU, CU, system clock and immediate access store

leadVisual.title: Components in one calculation

coreExplanation: The ALU carries out arithmetic and logical operations. The CU decodes the instruction held in CIR and generates the signals needed to move values and carry out the selected operation. These are processing and coordination roles respectively.

The system clock generates regular pulses that synchronise processor operations. One instruction can require several cycles. The immediate access store (IAS) is the main memory holding instructions and data available to the processor during execution; it is not the same as long-term secondary storage.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Address, data and control buses

leadVisual.title: A memory transaction

coreExplanation: The address bus carries the address that selects a memory location or an addressed interface. In the basic processor-controlled model it travels outwards from the processor. The data bus carries instructions and data between components and must support reads and writes.

The control bus is a set of coordinating signal lines. Read and write signals travel from the processor; signals such as interrupt requests travel towards it. Calling the control bus bidirectional describes the collection of lines, not a claim that every individual control signal travels both ways.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Factors affecting processor performance

leadVisual.title: Workload and limiting condition

coreExplanation: Processor type matters because instruction sets and internal organisation differ. Designs may use different instruction complexity, pipelining, cache arrangements and amounts of work per clock cycle. A comparison needs a specified workload; a higher clock frequency alone does not establish which different processor is faster.

Additional cores can execute independent tasks or parallel parts of a program concurrently. Sequential dependencies and communication overhead limit the benefit. A wider data bus can transfer more bits at once; a faster clock provides more cycles per second. Neither removes all memory or input/output delays.

Cache stores copies of recently or frequently needed instructions and data close to the processor. A hit avoids a slower main-memory access. Increased cache capacity can help when it retains more of the working set, but performance depends on access patterns and hit rate as well as size.

knowledgeUnits.heading: USB, HDMI and VGA connections

leadVisual.title: Port choice

coreExplanation: A port provides a physical and electrical interface for a peripheral connection. The device and computer need compatible signals and protocols. Adapters may convert signals; a connector that fits mechanically is not by itself proof of compatibility.

USB carries digital peripheral data and can provide power. HDMI carries digital video and audio to a compatible display. VGA carries analogue video and does not carry the display's audio. USB capabilities depend on the version, cable and devices, so one speed should not be assigned to every USB connection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Fetch using register-transfer notation

leadVisual.title: Instruction fetch: address and value transfers

coreExplanation: In this notation, [PC] means the contents of PC and [[MAR]] means the contents of the memory location whose address is in MAR. The arrow points towards the destination. MAR ← [PC] therefore copies the next instruction address into MAR.

The CU issues a memory-read signal; the instruction from the selected location travels to MDR and is copied to CIR. PC advances to the next sequential address. For these examples each instruction occupies one location, so the increment is one. Some fetch operations can overlap; the instruction must reach MDR before it can be copied from MDR to CIR.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Decode, execute and select the next instruction

leadVisual.title: Execution after decoding

coreExplanation: Decoding identifies the operation and interprets its operand. The CU then coordinates the transfers and ALU operation required for execution. Execution depends on the instruction: a load reads data, a store writes data, arithmetic calculates a result, and a jump changes the next instruction address.

The PC's sequential increment is not a guarantee that the next instruction will be adjacent. A taken branch can replace PC during execution. At the end of the cycle the processor checks for pending enabled interrupts before continuing the normal instruction sequence.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Purpose, causes and applications of interrupts

leadVisual.title: Event → useful response

coreExplanation: An interrupt is a request or event requiring the processor to suspend its normal instruction sequence and transfer control to a handler when the request is accepted. This supports response to asynchronous events without continually polling every device.

Requests may originate from hardware, such as a device completing input/output or a timer expiring, or from software requesting a system service. Exceptional conditions such as an arithmetic error also require processor attention. The precise treatment of faults depends on the processor; the basic taught sequence considers interrupt checks at instruction boundaries.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Detection, ISR and restoration of context

leadVisual.title: Handling sequence

coreExplanation: In the basic fetch-execute model, the processor checks for pending enabled interrupts after the current instruction finishes. Priority and interrupt-enable rules determine which request can be accepted. A lower-priority request can remain pending rather than being lost.

Before transferring control, the processor saves the return address and the state needed to resume the interrupted work. The appropriate Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) services the event and acknowledges or clears the request as required. On return, saved state is restored so normal execution can continue correctly. Registers used by the ISR must be preserved as required by the system's interrupt mechanism.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assembly language and machine code

leadVisual.title: Three representations

coreExplanation: Machine instructions are encoded as binary patterns understood by a particular processor. An instruction contains an opcode and, where required, operand information. Assembly language provides readable mnemonics and symbolic names for the same low-level operations.

An assembler translates assembly source into machine code for its target instruction set. An ordinary mnemonic instruction corresponds to a machine instruction; labels and data declarations organise the source and are not additional operations for the processor to execute. Source for a different instruction set is not automatically interchangeable.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Applying both passes of an assembler

leadVisual.title: Worked symbol table

coreExplanation: During pass one, the assembler scans the source, assigns locations and records labels with their addresses in a symbol table. It advances a location counter according to each instruction or data item's size and can detect errors such as duplicate definitions.

During pass two, the assembler uses the completed symbol table to resolve symbolic operands, translates mnemonics to opcodes and emits machine instructions and data. A forward reference is now resolvable even when its label appeared later in the source; a name that remains undefined is reported as an error.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Trace the executed instruction sequence

leadVisual.title: Trace fields

coreExplanation: Start a trace from the supplied PC, register values, memory contents and input. Fetch the instruction at PC, apply its exact operation, then record the resulting state. Record a row whenever an instruction executes; a loop therefore repeats rows for the same instruction address.

Use the branch condition produced by the preceding compare operation. JPE jumps when that comparison was True; JPN jumps when it was False. A skipped instruction has no trace row. END terminates execution and returns control to the operating system, rather than fetching the following data declarations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Instruction groups in the example instruction set

leadVisual.title: Five syllabus groups

coreExplanation: Group an instruction by the operation it performs. Movement instructions copy a value, arithmetic instructions calculate a value, and input/output instructions transfer character data between the program and its environment.

Control instructions alter the sequence of execution. JMP does so unconditionally; JPE and JPN depend on a comparison result. CMP and CMI are compare operations: they compare values without themselves jumping. END terminates the program and returns control to the operating system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Data movement: ACC, IX and memory contents

leadVisual.title: Data-movement instruction meanings

coreExplanation: An immediate operand supplies a value directly. The example syntax uses # for denary, B for binary and & for hexadecimal: #15, B00001111 and &0F denote the same value. A bare address instead directs an instruction to memory.

Data-movement instructions copy rather than consume their source. LDX adds IX to its address operand and then reads the contents at that effective address. MOV IX copies ACC into IX; it does not copy IX into ACC. STO writes ACC into memory while leaving ACC unchanged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Arithmetic, comparison, branches and character I/O

leadVisual.title: Operation forms

coreExplanation: ADD and SUB combine ACC with an immediate value or the contents of a direct address, retaining the result in ACC. INC and DEC increase or decrease the named register, ACC or IX, by one. When tracing, change only the register named or implied by the instruction.

CMP compares ACC with an immediate value or directly addressed contents; CMI compares ACC with indirectly addressed contents. Neither replaces ACC with the compared value. JPE tests whether the comparison was True (equal); JPN tests whether it was False (not equal). JPN is not a test for a negative number.

IN reads one character and stores its ASCII value in ACC. OUT outputs the character whose ASCII value is in ACC. For example, 65 corresponds to A: OUT with ACC=65 produces A, not the two printed digits 65. END returns control to the operating system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Worked program: loop, comparison and output

leadVisual.title: Complete execution trace

coreExplanation: The program below repeats DEC and CMP until ACC reaches zero. The same JPN instruction is taken after the first comparison and not taken after the second. The trace therefore includes two visits to each loop instruction.

The load after the loop replaces the loop counter with an ASCII value before OUT executes. Separate the value used for loop control from the later output value; a register's meaning can change during a program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Immediate, direct, indirect, indexed and relative addressing

leadVisual.title: Address versus value

coreExplanation: Addressing modes define how to obtain an operand or target. Immediate supplies the value itself. Direct uses the stated memory address. Indirect treats the contents at that address as a pointer to another location. Indexed adds an index-register offset to a base address before accessing memory.

Relative addressing forms an effective address from a PC-related base and a signed displacement. Use the PC base or convention supplied in the question; it may refer to a PC already advanced during fetch. The syllabus example instruction list does not specify a separate relative-jump mnemonic, so relative calculations here state the base and displacement explicitly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Logical, arithmetic and cyclic shifts

leadVisual.title: One-place shifts of 10010111

coreExplanation: A shift moves a fixed-width bit pattern left or right. Logical shifts introduce zeros at vacated positions and discard bits that leave the word. LSL #n and LSR #n shift ACC logically by n positions in the example instruction set.

Arithmetic shifts interpret the pattern as a signed two's complement value. Right arithmetic shift replicates the sign bit; left arithmetic shift introduces zeros on the right, like logical left, but can overflow. Multiplying by a power of two is valid only if the signed result remains representable; right shifting a negative odd value rounds towards negative infinity.

A cyclic shift (rotation) wraps the outgoing bit to the opposite end. It preserves the bit pattern's number of ones rather than introducing zero or repeating the sign bit. State the word width and direction before performing any shift.

knowledgeUnits.heading: AND, OR and XOR with immediate or memory operands

leadVisual.title: Operand forms and bit rules

coreExplanation: Bitwise operations apply independently to corresponding bit positions. AND produces 1 only when both bits are 1. OR produces 1 when at least one bit is 1. XOR produces 1 when exactly one bit is 1, so equal input bits produce 0.

Each of AND, OR and XOR supports immediate #n, Bn or &n forms, or a direct memory-address operand. The operation combines that operand with ACC and stores the result in ACC. For a direct operand, retrieve the contents of the address before applying the bitwise rule.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Monitor and control a device using masks

leadVisual.title: Masking actions

coreExplanation: A device interface can encode several states or controls in one byte. A mask selects the relevant positions: AND with a single 1 tests a bit, while OR with a single 1 sets it. Number bits explicitly; these examples use bit 7 at the left and bit 0 at the right.

A test should operate on a copy of the device value. AND changes ACC by clearing unselected positions, so reload the original value before an unrelated update. To set a control bit while preserving others, OR the original value with the setting mask and write the result back to the device register. AND with a zero at a selected position clears that bit; XOR with a one toggles it.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Labels for instructions and data

leadVisual.title: Two label forms

coreExplanation: The form <label>: <opcode> <operand> names the address of an instruction. The operand is omitted for an instruction that does not require one, such as END. A branch can use an instruction label as its target.

The form <label>: <data> names a location containing the given data. The label denotes the location's address, not its contents. Loading or storing through the label accesses that location; program execution must end or branch before falling into data declarations.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Why an operating system is needed

leadVisual.title: A request crosses software layers

coreExplanation: An operating system is system software that manages computer resources and provides services for application programs. It also provides a user interface, such as a graphical interface or command-line interface, through which the user can request operations.

An application can request a file operation through the OS instead of implementing its own controller for every storage device. Coordinating requests centrally lets applications share hardware while the OS controls which operations are permitted. Application software still supplies the task-specific behaviour, such as editing a photograph.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Memory management

leadVisual.title: A simplified allocation record

coreExplanation: Memory management keeps track of allocated and available main memory. When a process starts or needs more working space, the OS allocates memory; when the process finishes, that allocation can be released for reuse.

The OS also controls access to memory so one process cannot freely overwrite another process's instructions or data. Allocation answers where a process can store its working data; protection answers whether an attempted access is permitted. Allocating RAM does not itself save a file permanently.

knowledgeUnits.heading: File management

leadVisual.title: Opening a saved timetable

coreExplanation: File management maintains the organisation of files and directories, with information such as names, locations, sizes and ownership. It supports operations including creation, opening, reading, writing, renaming and deletion.

When an application supplies a path, the OS locates the corresponding file and coordinates the requested operation with storage services. File organisation gives programs a consistent way to retrieve data without needing to know the physical position of each stored block.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security management

leadVisual.title: One file, different permissions

coreExplanation: Security management authenticates users and enforces access rights. Authentication establishes an identity, for example by checking credentials; permissions determine which resources and operations that identity is allowed to use.

An OS can restrict a student to reading a shared document while allowing a teacher to modify it. An authenticated login therefore does not grant unrestricted access. Logging activity and applying security updates can also support protection of the computer system.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Hardware and peripheral management

leadVisual.title: Two documents share a printer

coreExplanation: Hardware management coordinates communication with input, output and peripheral devices. Device drivers translate general OS requests into commands understood by particular devices, allowing applications to use a consistent interface.

Devices and processors operate at different rates. Buffers hold data during transfers, and queues allow requests to wait until a device is available. An interrupt can notify the OS that a device has completed an operation or needs attention; the OS then arranges the appropriate response.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Process management

leadVisual.title: A possible single-core schedule

coreExplanation: A process is a program in execution. Process management records process states and schedules which ready process receives processor time. On one CPU core, switching between processes can give the appearance of simultaneous progress.

A process waiting for input or output cannot usefully continue that work. The OS can give processor time to another ready process, then allow the waiting process to continue when its event completes. Information about the interrupted execution must be retained so that each process resumes correctly.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Disk formatter

leadVisual.title: Disk formatter: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A disk formatter prepares a storage medium or volume with the file-system structures needed to organise files. Formatting establishes an empty organisational structure; it does not install all application software or restore a previous user's documents.

Reformatting an existing volume can make its current files inaccessible. A storage fault or a missing file is therefore not a reason to format a disk automatically; preserve needed data and choose the utility appropriate to the problem.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Virus checker

leadVisual.title: Virus checker: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A virus checker scans files, memory or activity for evidence of malware, using methods such as known signatures and suspicious behaviour. Its detection information needs updating as new threats are identified.

Detected items may be quarantined so they cannot run, removed, or repaired where that is possible. Detection does not guarantee that every new threat is found, and removing malware does not necessarily recover data it has already damaged.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Defragmentation software

leadVisual.title: Defragmentation software: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: On a magnetic hard disk, parts of one file may occupy separated blocks. Defragmentation relocates the file's blocks into fewer, more contiguous groups and can consolidate free space.

A magnetic drive's head can then need less movement when reading the file, reducing access delays. This explanation depends on mechanical seeking: an SSD has no moving read head, so routine HDD-style defragmentation is not the same performance treatment for an SSD.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Disk contents analysis and disk repair

leadVisual.title: Disk contents analysis and disk repair: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: Disk contents analysis can report how storage space is being used. Disk checking and repair tools examine file-system consistency and may detect problems such as lost allocation information or unreadable sectors.

A repair utility attempts supported corrections and can mark unsuitable areas to avoid further use. It cannot guarantee recovery from physical damage. Analysing a disk does not mean erasing it, and a recoverable backup remains valuable if repairs fail.

knowledgeUnits.heading: File-compression utilities

leadVisual.title: File-compression utilities: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: A file-compression utility encodes data in a representation that can use fewer bits. Smaller files can require less storage space and less time to transfer over a connection with a given data rate.

A general-purpose archive utility uses lossless compression so decompression restores the original file exactly. The reduction depends on the data: an already compressed or poorly compressible file may shrink very little or even gain overhead. Compression alone does not create a recovery copy or encrypt the contents.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Back-up software

leadVisual.title: Back-up software: input, operation and outcome

coreExplanation: Back-up software creates recoverable copies of files or system data. It may schedule copies, select changed files and retain versions so that an earlier state can be restored after deletion, corruption or equipment failure.

A useful recovery copy must remain available when the original is lost. Keeping the only copy on the same failing disk does not protect against that disk's failure. Checking that files can actually be restored is more useful than assuming a completed copy job guarantees recovery.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Program libraries and routine calls

leadVisual.title: Using a supplied square-root routine

coreExplanation: A program library is a collection of existing routines or modules that other programs can use. For example, a developer can call a supplied mathematical function or image-reading routine rather than implement the algorithm from the beginning.

The developer reads the routine's interface: its name, required arguments, returned result and any conditions for use. Testing the surrounding program is still necessary because a correct library routine can be called with inappropriate data or used incorrectly.

Reusing documented, tested code can reduce implementation and testing effort, improve reliability and provide specialist operations the developer would otherwise find difficult to create. These are benefits of suitable libraries, not guarantees about every file downloaded as a library.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dynamic linking and developer benefits

leadVisual.title: Two ways to deliver a routine

coreExplanation: With static linking, required library code is incorporated into the built executable. A Dynamic Link Library (DLL) remains a separate file whose routines are linked when the application is loaded or as they are needed during execution.

Several applications can use one compatible DLL instead of each storing its own incorporated copy. This can reduce duplication on disk and permit sharing of loaded library code in memory. The calling executables can also be smaller because that code is held separately.

A compatible correction to the separate library can be deployed once for its callers without recompiling each caller; running programs may need to be restarted or reload the library to use the update. The interface and behaviour must remain compatible. A missing or incompatible DLL can prevent loading or cause failures, so updates require checking.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Assembly source to target instructions

leadVisual.title: A small assembly routine

coreExplanation: Assembly language represents processor instructions using mnemonics and operands. An assembler converts a program written in that notation into the machine-code instruction encodings for its target processor; it does not translate high-level source such as Java.

The output may be a complete machine-code program or an object-code module that still requires linking. A linker combines modules and resolves references between them before a complete executable can be loaded. The instruction set determines which mnemonics and encodings are valid.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compilation before execution

leadVisual.title: Build and run are separate operations

coreExplanation: In the native compilation model, a compiler translates high-level source as a whole program or compilation unit into machine code before that code executes. Object-code modules can be linked into a complete executable. Some compilers instead target an intermediate representation, as in the Java example in the next lesson.

Translation diagnostics identify detected source problems. A source correction must be translated again before the built program reflects that correction. Successful compilation does not prove that the algorithm is correct or prevent every run-time error.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Translation during execution

leadVisual.title: Execution order is not just page order

coreExplanation: In the high-level interpretation model, an interpreter translates and executes statements as execution proceeds rather than first producing a separate permanent native executable for the complete source program. The interpreter itself is software running on the computer.

Execution follows control flow. A loop can cause the interpreter to process the same statement repeatedly; a branch can skip statements. An error encountered during execution can stop progress at that point. Partial execution and immediate feedback are useful when investigating a developing program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Compare approaches and justify a choice

leadVisual.title: Compare matching factors

coreExplanation: Choose by the required workflow rather than calling one translator universally better. An interpreter can provide immediate feedback while individual statements or incomplete program sections are tested. The environment must still support the source language and the required operations.

A native compiled executable avoids translating the original source on every run and can be distributed without that source. It can suit repeated execution or delivery to end users. A separate build is needed after source changes, and the produced native code must suit the target platform.

Interpretation can add execution overhead and normally requires the interpreter and an executable form of the program's source or intermediate code to remain available. Real tools may combine techniques, so a justified exam answer links the specified translation model to a concrete requirement instead of making an unconditional speed claim.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Java source, bytecode and the JVM

leadVisual.title: Two translation stages, one program

coreExplanation: Java illustrates partial compilation and partial interpretation. The Java compiler javac translates .java source into .class files containing bytecode. Bytecode targets the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), not one particular physical processor's instruction set.

A compatible JVM on the host executes that bytecode. It may interpret instructions and use a just-in-time (JIT) compiler for frequently executed code. The same suitable bytecode can run on different platforms with compatible JVMs, although platform-specific native dependencies can limit portability.

The source-to-bytecode build and the host execution are distinct stages. Installing a JVM does not by itself translate an edited .java file, and copying a .class file does not make it direct universal CPU machine code.
