knowledgeUnits.heading: Coding with context-sensitive prompts

leadVisual.title: What a coding prompt can show

coreExplanation: An Integrated Development Environment (IDE) brings programming tools into one working environment. While code is entered, context-sensitive prompts suggest suitable identifiers, keywords, members or parameters based on the current position and language context.

A prompt can reduce typing and help a programmer recall a routine's interface. The programmer must still select the intended operation and supply meaningful arguments; a syntactically available suggestion may be inappropriate for the problem.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Dynamic syntax checking

leadVisual.title: From a highlight to a correction

coreExplanation: Dynamic syntax checking examines source as it is entered and highlights violations of the language's rules, such as an incomplete expression or a missing keyword. Feedback before a full run helps the programmer locate and correct an error early.

An inline diagnostic can describe the detected problem and indicate its source location. Read the message with the surrounding statement to investigate its cause. A reported location can be where a problem becomes detectable rather than where the original mistake was made.

Syntax checking does not establish that the program solves its intended task. For example, a legal subtraction can still be wrong when the specification requires addition, so expected results and execution evidence are also needed.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pretty-printing and code folding

leadVisual.title: Presentation tools do different jobs

coreExplanation: Pretty-printing presents source in a consistent readable form, for example by indenting nested blocks and applying syntax colouring to keywords or other language elements. This helps a programmer recognise structure and spot suspicious formatting or missing elements.

Expanding and collapsing code blocks reveals or hides sections in the editor so attention can be focused on the relevant part of a large program. Folding changes the display only: hidden statements still belong to the program and execute whenever control flow reaches them.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Single stepping, breakpoints and inspection

leadVisual.title: State around one assignment

coreExplanation: Single stepping advances through execution one statement at a time, pausing so its effect can be examined before the next statement runs. This lets the programmer relate a change in program state to the instruction that just executed.

A breakpoint pauses execution when a selected location is reached, normally before that statement executes. Place it where relevant values are available and just before the suspect calculation or decision. Reaching a breakpoint does not itself correct the fault.

While paused, variable or expression inspection shows current values for comparison with the expected state. A report window displays information such as program output, run-time errors and diagnostic messages. Its output can be compared with the expected result after stepping an OUTPUT statement; inspecting a variable alone does not execute that output.

Use a deliberate loop of predict, execute one step, inspect and compare. If a watched value changes unexpectedly, inspect the statement that just executed and its inputs rather than placing unrelated breakpoints throughout the program.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Security, privacy and integrity

leadVisual.title: Classify the consequence

coreExplanation: Data security protects information against unauthorised access, loss or damage. Privacy concerns the appropriate collection, use and disclosure of personal information. Data integrity concerns accuracy, completeness and consistency, including avoiding incorrect changes during processing or transfer.

These concepts can be affected separately. Restricting access does not make an incorrect value true, and copying a record perfectly does not make its disclosure appropriate. Identify the property affected from what happened to the data, not simply from the presence of a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Protect the data and its processing system

leadVisual.title: Two independent protection targets

coreExplanation: A system must remain available to authorised users and must execute trusted operations. Malware, stolen credentials or damaged hardware can disrupt processing or expose data even when a separate file copy has been protected.

Data also needs protection wherever copies are stored or transferred. A secured computer cannot prevent disclosure from an unencrypted removable drive that has already been lost. Combine system controls with protection of the data and recoverable copies.

knowledgeUnits.heading: User accounts and passwords

leadVisual.title: Account login

coreExplanation: A user account gives a person a distinct identity on a computer or network. The system associates that identity with permissions and an activity record. Separate accounts help attribute actions to individual users.

A password is secret knowledge used to authenticate the claimed identity. The system checks the supplied password against the account's stored verifier before accepting the login. Hard-to-guess passwords and limits on repeated attempts reduce guessing; a disclosed password can still be misused.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Create and verify a digital signature

leadVisual.title: Digital signature: sender and receiver

coreExplanation: The sender applies a hash algorithm to a message to produce a digest, then signs that digest using the sender's private key. In the simplified signing model, this is described as encrypting the digest. The sender sends the message together with the digital signature.

The receiver uses the sender's public key to verify the signature; in the simplified model, decrypting the signature recovers the sender's digest. The receiver also hashes the received message with the same algorithm and compares the digests. A match supports the claimed origin and shows that the signed content has not changed, provided the public key is correctly associated with the sender.

A digital signature does not make the message unreadable. Confidentiality requires encryption separately. Signing the digest must not be confused with sending the private key or merely appending an unprotected checksum.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Biometric authentication

leadVisual.title: Capture and match a biometric

coreExplanation: Biometrics use a physical or behavioural feature, such as a fingerprint, iris, voice or typing pattern. A sensor captures the feature and software extracts a template that is compared with an enrolled reference.

A sufficient match authenticates the identity claim. False acceptance can admit an impostor, while false rejection can deny a legitimate user. Sensors and protected templates are needed, and a compromised biological feature cannot be replaced as easily as a password.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Firewalls on a PC and at a network boundary

leadVisual.title: Traffic decisions and firewall placement

coreExplanation: A firewall checks incoming and outgoing traffic against configured rules, for example rules about addresses, ports, protocols or connection state. It allows permitted traffic and blocks disallowed traffic; it may also log decisions.

A host firewall runs on one computer. A network firewall filters traffic passing through a network boundary. Neither arrangement guarantees that all harmful content is detected: permitted traffic can still carry a deceptive message or malicious download, and poorly chosen rules can leave unwanted access open.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-virus software

leadVisual.title: Respond to a suspicious executable

coreExplanation: Anti-virus software scans files, memory or activity for known virus signatures and suspicious behaviour. On detection it can block execution, isolate a file in quarantine, or remove the malicious code.

Detection information must be updated as new threats are identified. Quarantine prevents normal use of a suspicious file while preserving it for review. New or concealed malware may escape detection, so a successful scan does not prove that every file is safe.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Anti-spyware software

leadVisual.title: After detecting a keylogger

coreExplanation: Anti-spyware looks for software that covertly monitors activity or collects information. It can detect a monitoring component, stop it, quarantine it or remove it. Detection may be included within a broader anti-malware product.

Removing spyware reduces further collection but cannot retrieve information already sent to a third party. Exposed credentials may need replacing, and the entry route should be addressed to reduce reinfection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Combine controls for different risks

leadVisual.title: A travelling employee's computer

coreExplanation: Encryption changes readable plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and key. It protects the confidentiality of stored or intercepted copies; the authorised application needs the correct key to recover readable data.

Choose controls by mechanism. Login authentication checks identity, a firewall filters connections, anti-malware addresses malicious software, and encryption protects content outside normal access paths. Combining these controls reduces different risks without assuming that any one control replaces the others.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Viruses attach to a host and replicate

leadVisual.title: Follow an infected host

coreExplanation: A virus is malicious code that attaches to or modifies a host file or program. Running the infected host can execute the virus and allow it to replicate into further files. Its payload may corrupt information, delete data or disrupt the computer.

Networks, shared files and downloaded attachments provide routes for infected hosts to reach other computers. Avoid executing untrusted files and use maintained detection software to reduce this risk.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Spyware monitors and discloses

leadVisual.title: The collection and disclosure route

coreExplanation: Spyware covertly monitors activity or collects data, for example by logging keystrokes or recording the screen. Collected information may be sent to a third party, exposing private details or credentials.

Its defining feature is covert collection, not necessarily self-replication. Anti-spyware can address the installed component, while controlled installation and caution with downloads reduce entry opportunities.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Unauthorised access by hackers

leadVisual.title: Entry route and consequence

coreExplanation: In this security context, a hacker gains or attempts unauthorised access to a system or its data. Weak credentials, exposed services or unpatched vulnerabilities can provide an entry route.

The resulting access may permit disclosure, alteration or disruption. Strong authentication reduces impersonation, software patches address known vulnerabilities, and access rights limit what a compromised account can do.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Phishing persuades the user

leadVisual.title: A deceptive sign-in request

coreExplanation: A phishing message impersonates a trusted organisation or person and persuades the recipient to disclose information or perform an unsafe action. It may use urgency and a link to a fake sign-in page to capture credentials.

Check the request through an independently obtained contact or known website rather than the message's link. Filtering and training reduce exposure; multi-factor authentication can reduce the impact of a stolen password but does not make every deceptive request harmless.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Pharming changes the destination

leadVisual.title: Similar outcome, different route

coreExplanation: Pharming redirects a user to a fraudulent site, for example by corrupting DNS or local name-resolution information. The user may type the intended address correctly yet be directed to a different destination.

Protect name-resolution settings, update affected software and investigate certificate or hostname warnings. An HTTPS indicator alone does not prove that a site is legitimate; examine the intended destination and do not ignore a certificate mismatch.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Match precautions to the threat

leadVisual.title: Choose from the mechanism

coreExplanation: A useful precaution interrupts a specific route or reduces a specific consequence. Explain that link: patching repairs a known software weakness, permission restrictions reduce exposure, and independent verification challenges a deceptive request.

Controls reduce risk rather than eliminate every possible incident. Combining prevention, detection and recovery allows a response when one measure fails. Choose controls appropriate to the system and explain what remains outside each control's role.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Encryption and decryption

leadVisual.title: From readable data to a protected copy

coreExplanation: Encryption applies an algorithm and key to plaintext, producing ciphertext. Decryption applies the corresponding algorithm and correct key to recover the original readable information. An intercepted or stolen encrypted copy should be unintelligible to someone without the required key.

Protect the key separately from the encrypted copy. Encryption does not decide which logged-in user may edit a record, prevent deletion of ciphertext, or prove that the source data was true. Its main role here is confidentiality.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Apply access rights to data

leadVisual.title: Personnel-file permissions

coreExplanation: Access rights associate users or roles with permitted actions on a resource. Read permits viewing, modify permits alteration, and delete permits removal. A service checks the requested operation against these permissions after identifying the user.

Least privilege gives a role only the rights needed for its work. Restricting read access supports confidentiality; restricting changes supports integrity. Rights on a server do not protect an unencrypted copy outside that server, and authorised users can still make mistakes.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Validation and verification answer different questions

leadVisual.title: A source mark of 46 is entered as 64

coreExplanation: Validation tests whether input satisfies stated rules and is reasonable for its purpose. Verification checks whether information has been entered, copied or transferred accurately relative to its source. Both reduce the acceptance of errors and so help maintain data integrity.

A plausible wrong value can pass validation, and two copies of a false original can agree. Neither process proves that the source is true. Use both when a system needs acceptable values and faithful copying.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Range and limit checks

leadVisual.title: Apply the written bounds

coreExplanation: A range check applies both a lower and an upper bound, such as 0 <= Mark <= 75. Test both endpoints as well as values outside them; the stated rule decides whether the bounds are inclusive.

A limit check applies one upper or lower bound, such as FileSize <= 10 MiB. It does not introduce a second bound that was not specified. Choose a range when both ends matter and a limit when the requirement supplies one bound.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Format and length checks

leadVisual.title: Code rule: two uppercase letters, then four digits

coreExplanation: A format check tests a required pattern, for example two uppercase letters followed by four digits. A length check tests the number of characters, for example exactly six. The two checks ask different questions about the same string.
A six-character value can still have the wrong format. Check the complete pattern and the specified character count, preserving leading zeros when a code is a string.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Presence and existence checks

leadVisual.title: Stored customer IDs: C102, C107, C115

coreExplanation: A presence check requires an entry rather than a blank required field. An existence check looks for the supplied value in a specified stored lookup or file, such as checking that a customer identifier belongs to an existing customer.
A value can be present but absent from the lookup. Define which field is required and which stored set supplies valid identifiers; do not confuse these checks with a format test.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Calculate and check an identifier's check digit

leadVisual.title: Weighted check digit: a complete calculation

coreExplanation: A check digit is derived from the other digits in an identifier and stored with them. On entry or scanning, the system repeats the stated calculation and compares the expected check digit with the supplied digit. A mismatch causes rejection or re-entry.

Use the algorithm given in the question: different schemes use different weights and moduli. For the example here, multiply the four data digits by 3, 1, 3, 1 and choose a final digit that makes the total a multiple of 10. Some errors can still produce the same check digit.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Verify entered data

leadVisual.title: Source code: BK209

coreExplanation: For a visual check, a person compares the entered value with the original source and investigates differences. It is a comparison with a source, not simply a judgement that the value looks reasonable.

For double entry, the value is entered independently twice and the computer compares the entries. A mismatch is flagged for correction or re-entry. Agreement still cannot establish that the original source is correct, and repeating the same mistake can evade detection.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use parity on a byte

leadVisual.title: Build an even-parity byte

coreExplanation: A parity bit is chosen so the total number of 1 bits, including that bit, has the agreed even or odd parity. The examples use seven data bits and one parity bit to form an eight-bit transmitted group.

The receiver counts the 1s and compares the result with the agreed convention. Any odd number of flipped bits changes parity and is detected. An even number of flips can leave parity unchanged; the check alone cannot identify the incorrect bit or prove the byte is correct.

knowledgeUnits.heading: Use row and column parity

leadVisual.title: Locate a single-bit error by intersection

coreExplanation: Block parity organises transmitted groups into rows, applies a parity bit to each row, and adds a parity row or byte for the columns. The receiver checks parity in both directions using the agreed convention.

leadVisual.title: Copyright protects expression, including software code

coreExplanation: Copyright legislation is needed because software can be copied and distributed at very low cost while its creation requires time, skill and investment. It gives the copyright holder legal control over protected expression such as source code and documentation, including copying, distribution and adaptation, so unauthorised use can be challenged and creators can license work and receive revenue. Copyright protects expression rather than every abstract idea, and a limited legal exception is not permission for unrestricted copying.

A software licence is the copyright holder's permission to use protected work under stated conditions; paying for or downloading software does not normally transfer ownership. The licence may allow or restrict installation, copying, modification and redistribution. Copyright legislation establishes the rights, while the licence defines which of those acts the user is permitted to perform.

Copyright legislation is needed to give creators enforceable control over software expression that can otherwise be copied and distributed cheaply. A licence grants permission without normally transferring ownership. The required licence categories are the Free Software Foundation (FSF), Open Source Initiative (OSI), shareware and commercial software; justify a choice from the scenario's permissions, restrictions, support, cost and redistribution needs.

The Free Software Foundation (FSF) emphasises freedoms to run, study, modify and share software; source access is necessary for study and modification. The Open Source Initiative (OSI) defines open-source criteria and approves licences that meet them. Free/open-source software can still be sold and remains protected by copyright; users must follow conditions such as preserving notices, attribution or sharing derivative source under compatible terms.

Relational databases reduce selected file-based limitations by storing shared facts once in linked tables with centrally enforced rules.

A relational database addresses these limitations by separating entities into linked tables, storing shared facts once, identifying records with keys and enforcing relationships and constraints centrally. A DBMS supplies shared query processing, integrity, security, access rights and backup. These mechanisms reduce particular file-based risks; a relational design is not automatically smaller, simpler or error-free.

A file-based approach stores data in separate application files. The same fact may be repeated in several files or records, causing redundancy and wasted storage. Separate files may use incompatible formats, isolate data, duplicate validation/security code and make shared querying, concurrent access, backup and recovery harder to manage.

leadVisual.title: Referential integrity

coreExplanation: A one-to-one relationship links one record on each side. A one-to-many relationship links one parent record to many child records. A many-to-many relationship is normally implemented through a linking entity/table that creates two one-to-many relationships. Referential integrity prevents orphan records: insert, update and delete operations may be rejected or handled by a defined cascade/null policy, but must not silently leave an invalid reference.

A candidate key is a minimal field or field set that uniquely identifies a record. One candidate key is selected as the primary key. A secondary key is a field used as an additional retrieval or ordering route and need not be unique; it is not another name for an unselected candidate key. A foreign key refers to a key in a related table. An index is a lookup structure built on one or more fields: it can speed retrieval but uses storage and must be maintained after changes.

An entity is a real-world thing about which data is stored and is commonly represented by a table. A table contains records (tuples); each record describes one entity occurrence. A field (attribute) is one named property or column. These paired terms are related but should not be collapsed into one definition.

leadVisual.title: What does a DBMS provide?

coreExplanation: A Database Management System (DBMS) provides managed features that address file-based duplication, inconsistency, isolation and uncontrolled access. The features work together rather than acting as unrelated utilities.
A data dictionary stores metadata about tables, fields, data types, keys, constraints and relationships. DBMS tools consult this dictionary when checking definitions, queries and data values.

Data modelling represents the entities, attributes and relationships needed by the organisation. The logical schema turns that model into the table structures, keys, constraints and relationships visible to programs without depending on physical disk layout.

Data integrity rules reject invalid or inconsistent changes, for example an unmatched foreign key. Data security limits who can read or change data; access rights can be assigned to individual users or groups according to their roles.

Backup procedures copy recoverable database state, while recovery restores a consistent state after loss or failure. A backup is not an access-control substitute, and access rights do not replace recovery planning.

coreExplanation: Choose and justify a stack, queue or linked list from its LIFO, FIFO or linkage features. Add, edit and delete data in these ADTs and implement them using arrays; pseudocode for the ADT operations is not required by the syllabus.

An abstract data type (ADT) is a collection of data and a set of operations on those data. The permitted operations and their effects define the ADT; its internal storage can change without changing that behaviour. Stack, queue and linked list are examples of ADTs.

A stack is LIFO: add with push and delete with pop at the top. A queue is FIFO: add with enqueue at the rear and delete with dequeue at the front. A linked list stores data plus a next pointer/index in each node; start identifies the first node and null ends the chain.

All three can be implemented using arrays and state variables or indexes. Stack uses an array with a top/stack pointer; queue uses an array with front and rear; linked list uses Data and Next arrays (or an array of node records), start and a free list. Candidates must be able to add, edit and delete data conceptually, but the syllabus does not require pseudocode for these ADT operations.

coreExplanation: The terminology procedure/function interface, header, parameter, argument and return value, and explain the relationship between these terms.

A procedure header or function header names the subprogram and declares its parameters; a function header also declares its return type. The procedure/function interface is the information a caller needs to use the subprogram: its name, parameter list and types, and any returned value/type.

A parameter is the named variable in the header, while an argument is the actual value or variable supplied at a call. RETURN sends a function value back to the caller; output displayed by a procedure is an effect, not a return value.

A subprogram interface gives the caller the name, parameter list and types, and any return value/type. A procedure header or function header declares that interface; a function header also declares its return type.

coreExplanation: Clear Cambridge pseudocode uses meaningful identifiers, consistent indentation, complete Cambridge constructs and a traceable control path. Efficient pseudocode avoids unnecessary repeated work while preserving correctness.

Efficient pseudocode avoids unnecessary repeated work and selects a structure suited to the data and stopping rule. For example, total and count can be updated during one traversal instead of scanning the same array twice when both results are needed.

Efficiency does not justify incorrect bounds, hidden assumptions or compressed code that cannot be traced. A strong answer remains clear: initialise once, access only valid data, avoid redundant calculations and use meaningful identifiers and coherent constructs.

At AS Level, justify an improvement from the actual algorithm, such as fewer repeated passes or stopping a search once the target is found. Do not claim that shorter text alone proves a more efficient algorithm.

coreExplanation: Compare the principles, benefits and drawbacks of waterfall, iterative and Rapid Application Development (RAD).

Waterfall supports planned sequential stages and traceability but its limitation is costly late change. Iterative development reviews repeated versions but can need careful scope control. RAD uses rapid prototyping, time-boxing and user involvement; it may be less suitable or unsuitable where exhaustive assurance and stable architecture are required.

Waterfall completes planned stages largely in sequence and supports documentation and traceability, but late change can cause substantial rework. Iterative development builds and reviews repeated versions so evidence can refine later cycles.

Rapid application development (RAD) uses rapid prototyping, time-boxed development and frequent user involvement to obtain feedback quickly. It can suit an interactive system with available users, but speed and repeated prototypes can conflict with exhaustive assurance or stable architecture. Agile is related extension context, not a replacement for the named RAD model.

coreExplanation: A structure chart documents decomposition before coding. Each box names a module, procedure or function; hierarchy lines show which module calls another; labelled arrows show the parameters passed across an interface.

To construct the chart, put the controlling module at the top, split the task into single-responsibility subtasks, connect each caller to the modules it invokes, and label every data or control value passed.

Parameters make module interfaces explicit. An input parameter supplies a value needed by the called module, while an output or by-reference parameter carries a changed result back where that interface is intended.

To derive equivalent pseudocode, turn every chart box into a PROCEDURE or FUNCTION with matching formal parameters, then write calls in the parent modules using arguments in the same order and with compatible types.
The pseudocode is equivalent only if it preserves the chart's hierarchy, call relationships and parameter flow; merely listing module names does not implement the design.

leadVisual.title: Maintenance changes a system after it has been delivered

coreExplanation: Maintenance continues after delivery because faults are discovered, operating environments and rules change, and users request improvements. Corrective maintenance fixes faults in required behaviour; adaptive maintenance changes software for a new environment, platform, law or external rule; perfective maintenance improves functionality, usability, performance or maintainability.

Classify the reason for the change, not the code edited. The same module could receive a corrective change for a crash, an adaptive change for a new operating-system interface, or a perfective change for faster search and a clearer result display.

Test the enhancement with data that exercises the new path and rerun regression tests for existing paths. Correcting a fault is corrective maintenance; adding or improving requested functionality is an enhancement and may be perfective maintenance.

Every maintenance change requires impact analysis, controlled amendment, tests for the changed behaviour and regression tests for unaffected behaviour. Records should link the request, code change and test evidence.
